newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Britain urges Israeli moves to defuse crisis.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges Israeli moves to defuse crisis.

text.p: Britain urged Israel on Friday to defuse the crisis with the Palestinians by keeping a tourist tunnel in Jerusalem closed and by starting to withdraw its forces from the West Bank town of Hebron.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told reporters he would make the proposals at a meeting of the U.N. Security Council on Friday, which was called to debate the crisis and the threat it posed to wider Middle East peace efforts.

More than 60 people died in three days of violence in the West Bank and Gaza sparked by protest at Israel's opening of a tourist tunnel adjacent to al-Aqsa and the Dome of the Rock mosques, Islam's third-holiest site. The fighting, reflecting Palestinians' deep frustration with Israel's new right-wing government, further undermined the shaky peace process.
Rifkind, whose country is a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, said Israel should keep the tunnel closed to tourism for now as a "moratorium" that would reduce tension.

"It was done (opened) very easily, it could be reversed very easily," he said. He also said Israel should demonstrate wider support for the peace process by starting to withdraw its forces from Hebron as provided for in the accord between the Palestinians and Israel's former Labour government.

"A commitment to start that process in the very near future would be a positive endorsement of the peace process," said Rifkind, who warned on Thursday that efforts to build Middle East peace were on the verge of collapse.

He denied that he was taking sides in the crisis and said there was no point in the 15-nation Security Council doing so at its debate. But he expressed hope the Israeli government would show flexibility and added: "There is a lack of clarity as to the overall policy the Israeli government is pursuing."
Israel said on Friday it had closed the tunnel temporarily for security reasons, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rebuffed U.S. suggestions that he close it permanently.

Rifkind said a meeting between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was vital so that they could "provide leadership to their people." He also backed a proposal by King Hussein of Jordan to set up an international commission to investigate sensitive archaeological issues in Jerusalem, a holy city for three of the world's religions -- Christianity, Judaism and Islam.

Arab nations said they were preparing a resolution for the U.N. meeting calling on Israel to close the tunnel and keep its commitments under previous agreements with the Palestinians. But, despite widespread criticism of Israel in Europe and the Arab world, diplomats said the Security Council was unlikely to issue any condemnation of the Jewish state.

The United States, Israel's chief ally, refused to blame either side for the crisis and only reluctantly agreed to hold the council meeting on Friday. Washington can use its veto to block any resolution or statement condemning Israel.
The United States has been working frantically to arrange a meeting between Netanyahu and Arafat to salvage its five-year-old Middle East peace drive.
